why: Proper names holding a four-digit number that the anachronism check reads as a year. The check exists to catch a hallucinated future date, and none of these is a date, so each entry is an exemption and has to be justified on its own. This began as film titles, 2001: A Space Odyssey in a 1968 rentals table and Airport 1975 in a 1974 one. It then turned out that model numbers hit the same check: a 1978 page dropped the Budd SPV-2000 railcar over it, and a 1982 page dropped the arcade cabinet Robotron: 2084. Neither is a claim about the 2080s, so the list covers any proper name and the check no longer confines the exemption to the film section. The revue convention, where a 1935 page lists Broadway Melody of 1936, stays generative in the 'of YYYY' rule and needs no entries here.
rules: Two conditions, both required. The number must sit beside enough other text in the name to be unmistakable, and the exemption fires only when the full name string appears in the text, so a bare number never passes on its own. A work titled only with a number cannot be listed at all: Prince's 1999 is indistinguishable from a stray year, which is exactly what the check looks for, so a page wanting to name it must leave the failure standing and say so in its notes. The check matches four-digit numbers from 1000 to 2099 on word boundaries, which means some names need no entry: Miner 2049er is safe because the trailing letters break the boundary, and a two-digit title like 10 never matches.
